en: Inquiry and Discernment on the Bodhisattva Precepts,
composed by the junior monk Zhuhong of Yunqi Temple. Respectfully reciting the *Fayi* (Unfolding the Hidden),
every word emits radiance, articulating what Śākyamuni wished to say and revealing that which Tiantai had not yet expounded.
Where the spirit penetrates, the dreamer is suddenly awakened; where the sincerity is profound, the stone man sheds tears.

Its resonance is perfect and its purport far-reaching—it is truly a divine pearl among the jewels of the Dharma. Its facts are verified and its phrasing exquisite—it is indeed a wondrous medicine from the "Green Bag.

How could I not venerate it? What difference could there be between us? To manifest a demonic form at will and prattle on recklessly, pointing at my noble body to ask about a sore—is this not a grave offense?
I am like one with a cataract; knowing my eyesight has failed, I turn toward the golden lancet to seek its removal, my intent being to restore clarity.

I humbly pray that you will dispel my ignorance, for both humans and devas shall depend upon it. Written in haste and with some disorder, I hope you will forgive my rashness. With deepest reverence, I bow my head in the Chunxi era.

(1) Question: The fast and the precepts for communicating with the divine are the great laws of the Duke of Zhou and Confucius; they provide admonitions to instruct the common people and constitute the grand regulations of the sage-kings.

Now, if students already observe the Three Precepts (referring to abstaining from lust, anger, and greed) and embody the Four "Nos" (referring to the absence of arbitrary will, necessity, stubbornness, and self-centeredness), then these can be practiced throughout one's life, and the single mind will remain free from entanglements.
Furthermore, the Five Classics and the Five Elements each correspond to the Five Precepts; thus, they serve as provisional expedients for attaining Bodhi.
The practices cultivated by [the Buddha] have already reached their full realization, as praised by the Tiantai master Zhiyi.
Why must one turn away from the teachings of Mañjuśrī (Rutong) and bind oneself to the discipline of Vajrapāṇi (Huming)?
Answer: The prohibitions and precepts of Confucianism and Buddhism are largely similar, yet they differ in their degree of detail and strictness.

Take the five precepts as an example: the first is "not killing," which means to completely cease all killing. Confucianism, however, merely states that one should not kill oxen, sheep, dogs, or pigs without cause; it does not say "do not kill" outright.
It speaks of not using nets for fishing or staying overnight while hunting with arrows, but it does not say "do not fish or hunt. Thus, we know that the Confucian precepts...
The Confucian precepts accomplish mundane goodness; the Buddha’s precepts accomplish supramundane goodness. It has been so since antiquity that Confucians have received the Buddha’s precepts;
there is nothing extraordinary about this. Furthermore, an "emergent provisional bodhisattva" (chujia pusa) previously entered the ultimate truth.

Having proceeded from the ultimate to the provisional, they may act as they desire in both the mundane and supramundane realms without fail, never turning their backs on the Confucian youth while simultaneously upholding the Buddhist Vinaya. Moreover—
What is the obstacle?

(2) Question: Since the Daoist canon has plagiarized the Buddhist canon, then the Daoist precepts must likewise be identical to the Buddhist precepts. Receiving those golden rules is equivalent to our Brahmajāla Sūtra;
violating those blue regulations is equivalent to my *duṣkṛta* offense. Whether one is pure and bright or smeared with charcoal and mud, [it is like] the Big Dipper...
"The Grand Microcosm (Ta Wei) is analogous to the Hīnayāna; it seems difficult to adopt it wholesale, yet for the remainder, it is certainly appropriate to leave it as it is.
Answer: "The precepts of the Daoist Way appear distant from secular laws, yet in reality they are the same; they appear close to Buddhist laws, yet in reality they are different.

This is because the power of governance over all that is above and below heaven does not differ; however, there is a distinction between the mundane and the supramundane, and between the holy and the ordinary."
They are fundamentally distinct. Furthermore, consider this: although both the precepts of the Way and the Buddhist precepts involve ceasing evil and practicing good, their ultimate aims differ.

The former relies solely on cultivating stillness to solidify the vital energy (*qi*) and submerge the spirit, and through accumulating meritorious deeds to preserve the physical form and remain in the world. Thus, by upholding the precepts of the Way, one ascends to the Nine Heavens;
whereas by upholding the Buddhist precepts, one transcends the Three Realms. The golden rules of the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* cannot be discussed as being on the same level.
This is clear. (3) Question:
The Great Ming Code and its ordinances examined the statutes of previous dynasties. Our Sagely Ancestor was brilliant and wise, discerning the hidden recesses of human nature.
The King’s punishments are more severe than those in hell, and retribution is swifter than that in the life to come. Why, then, do people not comply? Furthermore—
He laid out the distinct precepts and replied:
"Retribution in the present life refers to the calamities of this world; in future lives, the wheel of suffering is inexhaustible. Persecution by kings is the misery of the physical body;
in hell, both wisdom and life are submerged together. Moreover, secular laws and punishments merely serve to discipline ordinary people within the worldly path."

This is still merely a secondary matter. However, it is exceedingly clear that the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* is intended for the true Bodhisattvas; within Buddhism, it especially belongs to the Mahāyāna, and thus cannot be discussed on the same level [as other texts].

(4) Question: The ancient precepts emerged in a world where no Buddha existed and were termed *śīla*. As natural precepts (*prakṛti-śīla*), they originally accorded with the human mind and required no formal observance.
To receive them now would surely nourish the dense forest of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Furthermore, it would expand the divergent views of sentient beings from the outset.
It is truly fitting to remain in profound stillness; why resort to such confusion?

Answer: If we speak loftily of an age without Buddhas and directly address the minds of people of the present, then not only would the Old Gautama have no words for the *vinaya*, and Upāli would be ashamed to recite the *karmavācanā*, but even the five divisions of the scriptures would be bound together and placed high on a shelf.
To remove the three robes and hang them from the tip of a tree is not in itself a transgression. If it were otherwise, I would only fear that the forest of Dharma is not dense;
I would simply worry that right view is not broad enough. Why should one be weary of such trivialities?

(5) Question: The marks of upholding the precepts like space were disparaged by Master Pang as those of a deluded person. Yet, Tiantai granted that one who can contemplate emptiness attains the Way and is fully endowed with it.
Being fully endowed, such a person transcends wisdom and praises sovereignty. How then can a deluded person differ from one whose precepts are deficient, broken, or pierced?

Furthermore, you say that the view of emptiness disturbs the mind, destroying the concentration associated with the precepts, and that an empty mind is heterodox and depraved, ruining [the practice]. How is this so?
I shall now settle my mind upon the discipline of restraint so as not to flow toward evil views. Furthermore, the Sūtra states:
"If there are those who attain emptiness, they will ultimately never violate the precepts. To what, then, does this refer?
Answer: Emptiness is of two kinds. If one accords with true emptiness, then the myriad dharmas are all complete; why would one need to further practice the Vinaya?

If one falls into a vacuous emptiness, then all virtues are destroyed; how could this not be injurious to the categories of precepts? To cling to such wild indifference and to treat ritual decorum with contempt—the error is great indeed.
(6) Question: It is said that those who have resolved their minds [to attain enlightenment] may be permitted to break the precepts; in the Mahāyāna, the transgression of precepts is tolerated.

This is perhaps because they possess skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) and are allowed to exercise their freedom in gathering and transforming sentient beings. Now, if one who maintains *dhāraṇīs* is already considered to be fully observant of the precepts, and one who maintains sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) is already considered to be fully observant of the precepts, and one who practices meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) is able to rescue others from the violations of the four grave offenses and the five heinous crimes—then [the Mahāyāna] is one.
The fixed [concentration] and wisdom are, conversely, placed before the *śikṣā* (precepts). A single incantation and a single phrase are sufficient to encourage the power of firm adherence.
Is it not because each has its own fundamental purpose?

Answer: The Bodhisattva who has resolved their mind possesses a resolve to uphold the precepts that exceeds that of the Śrāvakas by hundreds of thousands of millions of times. How could there not be [a difference]?

The principle by which transgressions and violations are permitted is truly because Bodhisattvas observe the opportune moment and exercise skillful means (upāya) to benefit sentient beings and aid all things;

they do not follow old precedents blindly, but rather establish regulations through intuitive synthesis. Such instances where there appears to be a violation but is not, represent the pinnacle of upholding the precepts.

Just as one who runs with his staff in hand is not called a traitor to his father, nor is one who pulls at the hem of the robe said to be disrespectful to the sovereign—these too are the pinnacle of loyalty and filial piety. As for the equivalence between the sūtras and dhāraṇīs:

The power of the precepts is likewise praised by the Tathāgata at various times and specifically highlighted according to particular circumstances; this is merely the standard method for expounding the Dharma.

Thus, at times he honors the Vinaya, wherein all a hundred modes of conduct are subsumed under the *vinaya*; at other times he esteems meditation (*dhyāna*), wherein all ten thousand dharmas converge upon right concentration (*samādhi*).

Host and guest alternate, and the capacities of sentient beings truly flow in two directions. One must not cling to fixed conventions and rashly give rise to dissenting opinions. If one relies on only one...
In representing the teachings of the school during this era, one proceeds from precepts to concentration, and from concentration to wisdom; thus, it is not the same as ordinary methods. (7) Question:

Regarding those in the home and those who have left it, what significance do outward forms and traces hold? Since that which is attained is non-attainment, how can one inquire about priority or sequence?

To manifest pure precepts, one speaks of having long since departed from worldly conditions; to encourage the profound mind, one points to attaining the Way in the prime of life. Thus spoke the Buddha.
"Your words provide sufficient proof; the earlier histories are difficult to rely upon. May I take it that this interpretation is acceptable? The answer was:
"To briefly set aside outward traces and obliterate the distinction between before and after—this is indeed how the principle holds.

Yet, since he has manifested himself as identical to ordinary beings, there must have been a time for his birth, a day for his renunciation, a season for his attainment of enlightenment, and a period for his preaching of the Dharma. How could these be conflated?"
It is not that the non-body manifests as a body; the body must conform to a constant form. It is not that the non-time manifests as time; time must accord with the sequence of the world’s history.
Furthermore, Confucius was called Rujiong and Laozi was called Kashyapa; these too were merely manifestations.
Nevertheless, beneath the pear tree at Changping and at the apricot altar of Hangu, their beginnings and ends are clearly traceable—these are precisely the examples thereof.

(8) Question: Regarding the transgression of precepts while without conscious intent (*acittaka*), since this constitutes a mitigation of the offense, those who seek such mitigation all train in being without conscious intent.
Without discrimination or restraint, they act according to their own whims and desires; they practice until even the "forgetting" is forgotten, appearing as if not intentionally committed.
Like dreaming within a dream, this must surely be a cause for karmic retribution.
Answer: Therefore, one seeks to diminish [the mind], yet when it is diminished, one cannot [sustain it]. As soon as one studies "no-mind," the mind immediately becomes "with-mind.
To transgress the precepts in such a manner—how could the sin be escaped? A true practitioner of cultivation should certainly not act in this way.

(9) Question: The Buddha’s mind is one of joyful relinquishment (*muditopekṣā*). Those who take his things act in accordance with his heart. While acts of robbery deserve punishment, those who seize only what remains after a theft should have their offenses reduced.
This is because he seeks the highest [enlightenment] above and transforms those below; why then are they classified under the same category as thieves?

If one observes through the perspective of the *dharmakāya*, stolen goods are the Buddha’s goods, and the Buddha’s goods are the goods of the world; since people steal from time to time, how can this not be so?

[Question: An offense is committed. [Answer: The Buddha has no intention of being stingy with things; yet the thief incurs guilt of his own accord. A father’s fundamental nature is one of loving his child;
yet the rebellious child inevitably incurs punishment. This is only natural. What intention could the Buddha possibly have? As for taking...
Regarding the property of thieves, there are two distinctions. One who acts out of a mind of compassion incurs no transgression and gains great merit;
one who acts out of a mind of greed commits theft equally by comparison. This has been definitively established in the commentaries on the sutras.
(10) Question: When a pig is driven to the slaughterhouse, the wheel of killing halts once its fixed karma has been manifested;
when the Buddha of Auspiciousness is set upon the sacrificial table for offering, the resentful energy of the victim sinks as the retribution for sin is apportioned.

To prepare a grand feast to nourish the sages and worthies—such that the sages can cause the one who cooks to feel no resentment—is this perhaps a way to resolve grievances? It is also, I believe, the skillful means (*upāya*) of a Bodhisattva.
Answer: When a Bodhisattva manifests killing, it refers to such acts as flaying, carving, hacking, and mincing, yet he never causes harm to even the most minute living being.
When sages and worthies partake of meat, it is said that eating it is the "stipend" of a great official, while not eating it is the "blessing" of a great official.
Only if one can truly kill without causing harm may one exercise skillful means (*upāya*). If one knows that there is merit...
As for those to whom one returns, one should naturally be cautious with one’s speech. To spend ten thousand coins on a single meal—this is something the wise do not do.
(11) Question: "The one mind is all minds; all minds are the one mind. The one precept is all precepts; all precepts are the one mind. All minds are the one precept;
all precepts are the one mind. Yet you ask: from what do precept and concentration arise?
Regarding the mental states [indicated], they appear to be incomplete. According to the first minor precept of the sutra, it specifies a mind of filial piety and a mind of compassion;
regarding the thirteenth precept against slandering and毁毀 (huidui), it likewise specifies a mind of filial piety and a mind of kindness and compassion.
Since these were indeed intended to be specified, why is it necessary to supplement them?
Answer: When one observes the fundamental substance of the mind-ground as a whole, that substance is but a single thought-moment, primordially and spontaneously perfected.

Yet, when the dharma-gates of the mind-ground are minutely analyzed, there are ten thousand variations, each of which may be assigned its own category. Thus it is said that the thirty stages of mind are all contained within a single hair-tip.
Furthermore, to further assign these to the characteristics of the precepts by means of the numbers one and two is like producing another hair-tip upon the hair-tip already mentioned.

For example, although a Heavenly King is titled the Great Lord, he must still appoint officials for the six ministries; yet even with these six ministries, the administration is not yet all-encompassing—does he not then further establish a hundred offices?
When the sutra initially mentions "such-and-such a mind" and "such-and-such a mind," it refers to the six ministries.
Now, when it further adds "such-and-such a mind" and "such-and-such a mind," it refers to the hundred offices. Just as these meanings are closely related, it should also allow for the rest...

This can be inferred by analogy; thus, it is easy for beginners to understand and simple to practice. For the wise, it requires nothing more than the spiritual integration and mental realization of the meaning.
(12) Question: The mind-ground naturally accords with principle; the mind-ground spontaneously attains what is appropriate. The nature of Buddha-nature is the nature of human nature.
Buddha-nature is eternally abiding; human nature is eternally abiding. Should one, therefore, first cause light to emanate from the mind-ground?
The Buddha-nature gives rise to its functioning. What principle would not accord with this? What matter would be unsuitable for it?
Why must one close one's eyes and borrow sight from Kāśyapa, or consult a map to seek a horse in the *Prātimokṣa*?
Is it because relying on the fifty-eight jewels of others leads to poverty once they are exhausted, while concealing one’s own thousand billion pearls and hiding them away is of no benefit?

Answer: Although the substance of the mind contains all phenomena, they are only known through their manifestation; although the earth possesses a thousand flowers within its seeds, they only bloom when the time is right.
It is like laughing at the poor man who borrows jewels, for if one does not know how to use them well, even a wealthy household can be established.

It is like envying the strongman who carries a pearl in his breast, for if he does not know not to point at it, the wondrous treasure will ultimately remain hidden. Thus, while the painting is not the actual horse, one must recognize the horse in the painting.

Relying on this excellent plan, one’s eyes do not depend on others. Just as one can have cataracts removed from the eyes by depending on another, so too does one take the mind as the precept by depending on profound discourses that exhaustively investigate the principles;
and by depending on the precepts to gather the mind, one obtains the true and efficacious medicine for curing illness. How could one possibly neglect this?
(13) Question: To not manifest [the truth], to not take vows, and to not train in the Buddha’s teachings is for oneself to be muddled.

To teach perversely and speak erroneously, failing to transform sentient beings, is for others to be muddled. To be muddled oneself and cause others to be muddled—how could this be merely like leaning against a counter to sell wine?
How is it any different from pointing at the Buddha while slandering him? Yet you call this a "light defilement"; in truth, I do not understand.

Answer: Regarding "not vowing" and "not aspiring," this does not mean they were entirely unaware of advancing on the Path; rather, it is because the mind of courageous vigor has not yet been aroused that noble deeds are difficult to accomplish.
Regarding "deviant teachings" and "deviant explanations," this does not mean they were entirely unaware of benefiting sentient beings;

rather, it is because their methods of guidance have not yet been refined that the merit of transformation cannot be realized. There is indeed a reason for not exposing grave transgressions but merely listing minor faults.
(14) Question: Regarding the Dharma of renunciation, one seeks the Dharma without bowing to kings; one seeks the Dharma without bowing to parents. The Dharma does not reside therein.
One need not revere the six types of close relatives, for the Dharma does not reside therein. One need not pay homage to ghosts or spirits, for the Dharma does not reside therein.
One simply knows that the words of the Dharma Master are trustworthy, and thus travels a hundred or a thousand *li* to bow before them.
Regarding the seeker of the Dharma (the Dharma Master...), one should provide such an explanation. Now, the Commentary says: "All those within the borders of the realm are subjects of the King;
there is no second sovereign other than the World-Honored One. How could one not pay obeisance? The Sūtra says: "Guarding the Buddha’s precepts is like serving one's parents;
the fourfold assembly sits in lower seats, just as they are filial and obedient toward their parents. How could one not pay obeisance?"
Furthermore, the Great Sūtras extensively expound the Way of Filial Piety, yet you show contempt for your parents; the Great Assembly is headed by the King, yet you show contempt for your sovereign.
Is this truly in accord with the Buddha’s intent? Suppose your father or sovereign were to receive the precepts and attain the Way—would bowing to them then diminish your merit?
Not so. Since the Buddha worships the Buddha, this is the practice of Constantly Non-Disparaging; why must one distinguish it again and again, as Huiyuan of Donglin did?
Answer: The name "Sangha" signifies "one who has left home. The Way of the Sangha is called "transcending the world. To leave home is...
One should not restrict this to the regulations governing family members and fathers; when transcending the world, one does not abide by the worldly laws of the rites between sovereign and subject.

This is because it is the sovereign and father who revere the Buddha and extend that respect to his monastic followers; it is certainly not the case that the monastics rely on the Buddha to treat the sovereign and father with contempt.
As for the Way residing in the sovereign and father, the ritual itself is rightly called the "Way of Ritual. Sentient beings are...
To bow before a Buddha is, in itself, called "bowing to the Buddha. There is nothing inherently improper in this. As for what we should do today, it simply depends on the circumstances.
If the time values the Buddha-dharma as paramount and grants us leniency by saying, "Do not prostrate," then one may follow the internal teachings [of Buddhism].
If the time values human ethics as paramount and establishes a fixed rule saying, "One must prostrate," then one should follow that.
It is permissible to follow royal regulations. On what is this based? The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "A bhikṣu who violates royal regulations incurs an offense.

The *Zhu jing yao ji* (Essentials of Various Scriptures) says: "Fools perversely practice the teachings of the Dharma and transmit them to others in succession, claiming that one should not prostrate to parents or honored relatives.
This does not accord with the intention of the Sages; instead, it invites the sin of ignorance. The sūtras and śāstras repeatedly clarify this point, which is sufficient [to refute such views].

According to the *Erlu* (Account of the Ears): "Is it not then the case that Huiyuan was in error? He replied: "At that time, the protocols for prostration had not yet been settled, so [the matter] was debated between the monastics and the laity.
Huiyuan’s correct argument was not biased; it was only logical that it should have been thus. What fault is there in this?"
(15) Question: Regarding these precepts, those who receive them must possess a mind and sentience; those who violate them are equal to wood, stone, or a wooden head.
Furthermore, it is said that "all earth and water were my former bodies, and all fire and wind are my original substance.
May the transmission of the precepts extend even to former bodies, and may the reception of the Dharma reach even the original substance?
The "Beauty Grass" (Meirencao) moves its stems to the rhythm of songs; this may be due to karmic ties of lust. The stone of Master Daosheng nodded when hearing the sutras;
how could it lack Buddha-nature? Please grant them ordination.

Answer: The discourse on earth, water, fire, and wind merely serves to clarify that sentient beings and insentient things alike receive their nature from the same source and share a single mechanism for sensation and response.

Therefore, to kill another is to kill oneself; there is no difference between killing an animal and killing a human. How could it be said that wood and stone are of the same category as those capable of thought and cultivation?
Even if a holy monk were to preach again before a rock, it would not necessarily fail to remain stubborn. As for the madman [who claims otherwise], his words are reckless.
Singing by the side of the grass—how could one possibly learn to strike the sandalwood drum again? As for the fact that when a single person awakens to the truth, empty space itself vanishes;

even down to the teaching of the insentient and the attainment of Buddhahood by the insentient, there are clear and explicit records of this. It is further said: "If a person recognizes their own mind..."
The great earth has not a single inch of soil. Since soil is identical to mind, so too are water, fire, and wind. One is originally a Buddha;
why then seek to attain Buddhahood?
(16) Question: Attending to the sick is indeed an expression of filial piety and compassion. Yet, my own body is likewise a vessel for sages and worthies.

Considering how difficult it is for a blind turtle to find its way through the hole of a floating log, and reflecting on how difficult it was for Bian Que to pierce the wall [of the Yellow Emperor’s palace], one must ask:
why should one willingly provide useless massages or subject oneself to the contagion of a terminal plague? A bodhisattva should surely know the proper means (*upāya*).
Answer: The field of merit is unsurpassed. It is indeed the firm duty of a benevolent person to prioritize the care of the sick.

While there are many gates to wisdom, how could a sage lack the philosophy of preserving one's own body? Whether attending to them personally, employing others, utilizing wealth, or exerting effort—all these are acceptable.
The Śākya-muni employed cotton wool to heal an illness; thus, physical touch is not necessarily without efficacy. Kongzi’s son remained in a perilous situation yet preserved his life;
how could he have been inevitably infected by pestilence? It is because saving others is an urgent matter that one feels compelled to act, unable to desist.

This is not like recklessly undertaking hardships for their own sake, acting when it could have been avoided. Furthermore, the "pity-field" (beitian) of antiquity and the "nursing and relief" (yangji) of today are both institutions of sagely rulers.

A loyal minister’s great compassion lies in his diagnosis of the illness; why must he necessarily suck at abscesses or press upon leprosy to be considered providing relief, or taste medicine and feed food to be deemed diligent?
(The story of Kong'er mentioned on the previous page appears as the account of Yu Xiang in the "Matters and Meanings of the Precepts Commentary"; let this be examined.)

(17) Question: To sell children and grandchildren to provide for the assembly, or to barter disciples while practicing compassion—claiming they have come for the sake of the Dharma and thus calmly accepting payment—is this not a light offense of defilement (*āpatti*) even if they have already awakened the aspiration for Bodhi?

How can a practitioner of the Way engage in such light trade? Those who travel south in search of the Way would be chilled to the core, and parents would surely follow them in search, receiving [the proceeds] as offerings.
"Human beings are like those in prison; how can they be so utterly lacking in skillful means? [The questioner] asks:
"The ancients spoke with earnestness to bestow instruction and used perilous words to demonstrate their sincerity. There are expressions that are true in word but not entirely so in reality.

When one reaches the height of gratitude, one says 'engraved upon the flesh and carved into the bone. How could there truly be such a matter as piercing the skin with a needle or carving it with a blade to express it?"
To speak of the ultimate sincerity of one's heart as "exposing one's gall and liver" does not necessarily mean overturning one's internal organs.

Even if one were to sacrifice their body for the Dharma or exhaust their life in honoring the worthy, such acts are merely the standard conduct of a Mahāsattva. To bring along one’s wife and children while serving a Brahmin is [a different matter].
Having nine sons and two daughters, he supported a plowman. It is said that while there were lofty models in antiquity, none have followed in their footsteps today.
(18) Question: Shanhui called himself a Mahāsattva; Zhigong identified himself as Avalokiteśvara; Wenling broke his precepts and burned his body;
Da Hui sought favors through his nephew by improper means. All of these violated minor precepts yet attained great reputations. Is this not each a case of karmic correspondence?
"Is this within the realm of principle?

He replied: "Ordinary people among the sensory objects may perhaps be constantly evaluated; however, extraordinary individuals beyond the mundane should not be discussed in terms of their outward traces.

When first born, pointing to heaven and pointing to earth, it did not hinder his being the Tathāgata. When about to die, silently entrusting and silently transmitting, what obstacle was there to his own [realization]?"
He is named a Bodhisattva and is already designated as Maitreya; he points far toward perfect penetration—what is there that is not permissible?

Furthermore, Wēnlíng Shànfā elucidated the hidden meanings of Bhaiṣajyarāja and did not, of his own accord, cast away his physical body. The Elder Gǎo did not diminish the tradition of the Linjì school; how could it be said that he had not yet eliminated affection and attachment?

It is simply that when it is appropriate to remain obscure, one remains obscure; when it is appropriate to manifest, one manifests. At times one maintains the constant, and at times one exercises expedient means.
Transformation. One should not regard [others] with self-praise and disparagement of others. How could those who violate reason and transgress the law be considered peers?
(19) Question:
Before five years of summer retreat (*varṣa*), one should specialize in the Vinaya; after five years of summer retreat, one may listen to the teachings and practice Chan meditation. This...

This pertains to the Hīnayāna and does not refer to those of great capacity. That he now recites it at each of the six periods of the day suggests that, in order to prevent the teaching gate and the meditation gate from being obstructed, this must be a case where a single dharma is integrated throughout—uninterrupted from the stage of the mind-ground to the stage of the ground itself. (Regarding "fáng" [prevent], some read it as "fáng" [obstruct]; let this be examined.)

Answer: He was a man of truly vast capacity and extraordinary proportions. He was not bound by whether it was after or before the summer retreat; he was naturally responsive, manifesting both smallness and greatness.

As soon as he maintained the precepts, he had already mastered the full texts of the teachings; upon correctly receiving the *vinaya*, he immediately awakened to the subtle purport of the Chan school.
When establishing himself, he caused the myriad dharmas to flourish without hindering the six periods of daily practice; when sweeping away delusions, he eliminated even the most minute traces.
How could even a speck of dust remain for a single thought? Master Huiyuan’s daily prostrations were constant; Master Yongming’s personal practice was never deficient.
How could they have been constrained by inferior faculties or treated as trivial matters? May all of us later students reflect deeply upon this.

(20) Question: The Buddha’s mind penetrates the three periods of time, and his great light fills the ten directions. How could he not know that the scriptures have entered China and that the flow of the Dharma has vibrated through Zhendan?
That the fragrance of incense and the flavor of pungent spices both follow the customs of the land of the Five Indias;

yet that the precepts and the rules of discipline have not fully cleansed the defilements and sins of the Nine Provinces. To hate them leads to slander; to leave them as they are leads to laxity. [This concerns] the Buddha’s Mound.
The *Nanshan* [Lüshi chunqiu] is thus deficient; it seems that the Confucian classics and the royal statutes should complement one another.

Answer: Although the Buddha’s mind penetrates the three periods of time, his remedies for defects are provisionally based on a single era. Although the Buddha’s light fills the ten directions, [his teachings are adapted to specific times].

If one seeks to gain trust, one must first follow the customs of one's own land; once the time is ripe, its influence will naturally extend afar. It is fitting that this be applied by analogy to other regions.
Thus, while the Confucian classics and royal statutes may seem difficult to employ concurrently, there is no harm in their dual practice when circumstances and conditions are favorable.

The Dharma indeed evolves in tandem with the world, and ritual propriety likewise arises based on righteousness. Some may say that the Vinaya differs from the Sūtras, just as worldly [customs differ].
The laws and regulations are established by a single person; even Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana could not have contributed to them.

Nevertheless, while the profound voice from the golden mouth cannot be praised in even a fragmentary word by an ordinary person, what harm is there if a clever craftsman mends a single thread in a small tear in the imperial robe?

Therefore it is said that by making a pact with a friendly state, one will surely be victorious in war.
Those who are called "excellent ministers" today were what the ancients called "thieves of the people."

Answer: The term "reciting the precepts" (śīla-uddeśa) does not refer to the kind of exposition given on ordinary days; rather, it refers to the recitation performed every half-month.

When the Saṃgha collectively performs the Poṣadha (Uposatha) every half-month, the monks themselves acknowledge their own transgressions and reveal their faults to one another. Fearing that this might inevitably give rise to heterodox slander, the rule was established that, with the exception of the sovereign, no other person is permitted [to preside].
As for the expansion of the scriptural texts and the proclamation of their profound meanings, these are matters distinct from the formal recitation of the precepts.
What fault could there be in this? To guide the deceased and to dispel misfortunes and hardships, all say that one must read and recite with a sincere heart;
they do not hear of anyone concealing the volumes in secrecy. To benefit others in this way accords precisely with the Buddha’s mind; this is called the gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*).

Answer: This refers to the meaning of sequential arrangement (*xingbu*) and perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*). That the patriarch is not the father, and the father is not the son, is the meaning of sequential arrangement.
That the patriarch, father, son, and grandson intersect and cooperate together is the meaning of perfect interfusion. It is like weaving brocade, where a thousand threads are joined;

(4) Question: Among the stages of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), the first is said to be "observing and penetrating to the source, bottom, and limit of ignorance (*avidyā*);

From this, one knows that by the stage of Equal Enlightenment, ignorance has been entirely severed and exhausted. Why is this so?
What is the doctrinal meaning? It is said that the ten stages (daśabhūmi) eliminate forty grades of ignorance.

Furthermore, the elimination of one grade is called Equal Enlightenment (samyaksaṃbodhi), and the elimination of another grade is called Sublime Enlightenment (pratyakṣabuddha). Together, they eliminate forty-two grades. Both of these meanings originate from the Wise Ones (jñānin).
There is a slight difference. How can they be harmonized? Answer:

In the stage of Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi), ignorance has already been exhausted; yet, that which remains to be severed is also ignorance. When both [the exhaustion and the remaining] are severed, they are equally non-existent.

This is called "further severance. It means that through the knowledge of equal enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), one severs delusions; through wondrous enlightenment (*pratyaksa-bodhi*), one severs the very act of severing.
Only when one is able to sever the act of severing can it be called the eternal severance of all ignorance. Thus, by severing the forty-two grades of delusion, one enters wondrous enlightenment.

(13) Question: Flowers represent the cause, while reality represents the fruit. Why, then, do the flowers offered to Śākyamuni not represent the cause?
Answer: Cause and effect are perfectly distinct; it is simply that you gentlemen fail to perceive them. This sutra takes the mind-ground as its central principle.

There is not a single dharma that does not flow from the mind-ground, nor is there a single dharma that does not return to the mind-ground. Such is the case with the myriad practices of the Bodhisattvas.
If it did not originally arise from the one mind and now returns to the one mind, it would not be called the cause of Buddhahood, nor would it be called the fruit of Buddhahood.
Now, these flowers emerge from the *citta-bhūmi* (mind-ground) of Vairocana; they symbolize that the Bodhisattva brings forth immeasurable causal practices from within his own mind.
By offering these flowers back to that Buddha, they symbolize that one completes the Buddha who is the fruit of one's own mind through the causal practices of one's own mind.

According to the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, the cause encompasses the fruit and the fruit penetrates the cause; they are not separate from cause and fruit, yet they do not fall into the category of cause and fruit.
When things are brought forth, there is nothing that cannot be offered to the Buddha; when phenomena are raised up, there is no dharma that cannot serve as a cause.

If one insists that a flower must represent the cause, this is not the meaning of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao). Why is this so? Sometimes a flower represents the cause and the fruit represents the result; it is only after the flower has blossomed that the fruit is formed.
Therefore, sometimes the cause is expressed as "reality" (śubha) and the fruit as "flowers," because flowers arise only after the seed has been planted.

Sometimes the cause is fixed as "concentration" (samādhi) and the fruit as "wisdom" (prajñā), because of the attainment of pure, ultimate, and pervasive illumination. Sometimes the cause is "wisdom" and the fruit is "concentration," because when delusions are shattered, the mind becomes tranquil.
How could evil be grasped through a single path, or discussed according to a single category?

Yet it is said that it manifests spontaneously of its own accord.
Answer: The Tathāgata’s wondrous samādhi is neither moving nor still, yet it is constantly moving and still; it neither emerges nor enters, yet it constantly emerges and enters.
This samādhi is named "Empty Essence" (Śūnyatā-svabhāva). Because emptiness is the counterpart to reality, it prevents the essence from being non-empty.

It would be like a mountain not admitting a mountain or a stone not containing a stone—merely a single state of dull stagnation. Since its essence is fundamentally empty space, Huaguang [the Flower Light] is thus at ease.
Manifestation! How could it be that once one has entered samādhi, one must simply be reduced to ashes and cease to exist?

In the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*, the Tathāgata enters the Samādhi of the Great Luminous Treasury (*Mahāprabhāsagarbha*) and yet manifests a pure land, engaging in mutual dialogue with the twelve great bodhisattvas;
what does this mean? Furthermore, there are hundreds of thousands of millions of names for samādhi; it is not merely a single flavor of quiescent stillness. Therefore...
There are samādhis whose names even the followers of the Two Vehicles have not heard, and whose meanings Bodhisattvas have yet to understand.

If one clings to a stagnant silence, then even the "Lion’s Bound" (*siṃhavijṛmbhita*) and "Lion’s Roar" (*siṃhapraṇāda*) samādhis would become mere clamor. He asked again: "All samādhis have entry and exit;
why is it that entry and exit are mentioned only in this context? He replied: "Entry and exit are not difficult [to understand] on their own."

This is difficult to achieve. Those of the Two Vehicles must withdraw their thoughts to enter and arouse their thoughts to emerge; thus, they cannot be said to possess mastery. Only when one attains mastery over the mind can it be called the "wondrous samādhi.

According to the *Avataṃsaka*, entering and emerging occur simultaneously; the environment and its inhabitants, as well as the primary and secondary fruits of retribution, interpenetrate in perfect fusion in an inconceivable manner.
This [attainment of the Two Vehicles] is merely a minor matter; how could it be considered extraordinary?
(15) Question: The Buddha said, "I have now come here eight thousand times," yet this merely symbolizes the Dharma. How can it be considered a literal statement? Answer:

If we rely on the gate of symbolic representation, then every phrase and every word is nothing other than a symbol. However, if we rely on the manifestation of practical application, what harm is there in taking it as a literal statement?
Indeed, among all the sūtras spoken by the Buddha, there is not a single dharma that does not integrate both phenomenon (shi) and principle (li).
The manifest and the real are both present. To speak of the manifest necessarily implies the real; to cite the real means that the manifest is contained within it.
As for this reciprocal movement, why should one be startled or find it excessive?

Laozi was once a ruler who did not emerge from the world, and Yunmen was three times a king—these were all actual realities, not merely symbolic teachings. Why, then, should the Tathāgata’s eight thousand returns alone be considered non-existent?

Regarding these matters: if the Tathāgata’s repeated coming and going already purely symbolizes that which is not real, then does the Huayan’s layered Dharma-realm also purely symbolize that which is not real?

A Buddha-activity as a flower in the sky, a site of practice as the moon in water—within the light of the Dharma-nature, revolving ten thousand ways and a thousand turns, such events are utterly ordinary;
they are entirely without anything extraordinary. Why doubt them? Why be startled? Furthermore, it is asked: the commentary says this points crosswise.
Regarding the assembly: the present ten locations do not equal those in other directions; the vertical clarification of coming and going does not encompass the aeons within a single atom.
How, then, can this be called the vastness of the Tathāgata’s compassionate vows? Answer: This means that by borrowing what is finite, the infinite is manifested.

In praising the Buddha, he is called "One of Ten Thousand Virtues. How could ten thousand exhaust the Buddha? In addressing the people, they are called "the Hundred Families. How could a hundred exhaust the people?
Although it is said there are ten locations and eight thousand [spheres], this signifies that horizontally there are no boundaries and vertically there is no end.
(16) Question: The commentary mentions two meanings of the lotus: being unstained while dwelling in turbidity, which serves as a metaphor for Vairocana abiding in impurity without being defiled;
this illustrates his virtue through analogy. However, it only constitutes one meaning [of "stopping"]. What are the two meanings?

Answer: There are two meanings. First, the flower necessarily dwells in turbidity and does not dwell on high plateaus; this is a metaphor for the Buddha manifesting his residence in a defiled land rather than a pure land.
Second, although the flower dwells in turbidity, it is not defiled; this is a metaphor for the Buddha dwelling in a defiled land without being stained by it.
(17) Question: Commentators on the scriptures of the past each had their own school of thought. As we now interpret this scripture, upon which authority should we rely?

If there were a separate authority to follow, one should not rely on the Tiantai commentaries; yet if there were no authority at all, it would be nothing more than a diffuse and arbitrary fabrication.
I pray that you will provide a clear exposition.

Answer: There are three propositions here. First is the primary school; second is the inclusive school; third is the school without a school. As for the "primary school," it refers to the Chan school.
This school takes the mind as its primary tenet. The mind is the progenitor of all scriptures and the source of the myriad dharmas.
The two characters "mind-ground" (*xindi*) encompass the Bodhisattva precepts without exception. Furthermore, this mind is precisely...
Because it is the Great Avataṃsaka, it is said to encompass both the fundamental principle and its manifestations.

For those who have realized the mind, not only are the colors of the vase, the ring, the hairpin, and the bracelet all gold, but even the grasses, trees, tiles, and pebbles are nothing but gold. The Āgamas and minor teachings are but the partial gates of external paths.
If one employs them with skill, they all perfectly fulfill their intended meaning; how much more so when the Tiantai teachings rely upon and follow them? Who could say this is impossible?
For my own school’s doctrine gives rise to those commentaries, as the Tiantai teachings do not transcend the mind.

To insist on setting up the flagstaffs of different schools in a rigid, vertical fashion, each refusing to yield to the other, would be like biological brothers harming one another—an act of great rebellion.

Regarding the statement "having no tenet": because the essential nature and characteristics of the mind cannot be found when sought, one constantly takes the mind as the fundamental principle (zong) rather than taking the mind itself as a tenet.
Therefore, it is said that even that which is called the "ground of the mind" is unattainable. Furthermore, he asked:

"Since you speak of the Chan school and also of the Huayan [Avatamsaka], and since the five teachings of Huayan place Chan at the level of the Sudden (dun), how is it that the Sudden is not yet separated from the Perfect (yuan) by more than a single gap?"
It may be said that both [systems] can be cited together. The answer is: Qingliang’s praise holds that the principles and tenets of Tiantai’s Four Teachings are perfectly complete;

however, the Five Teachings system adds the "Sudden" (Dun) teaching to supplement what was incomplete in the Tiantai system. Since there was no suitable place to assign the single school of the Dharma Treasure (Damo), it was provisionally judged to be subsumed under the Sudden.
Yet, in reality, the Sudden has two meanings: first, the merely sudden (dandun); second, the perfect-sudden (yundun). This Chan school is precisely the perfect-sudden.
Sudden. Yet why is it not called "Perfect" (Yuan)? It is truly because it focuses exclusively on directly pointing to the nature of mind to shatter the gradualist school.

Although the meaning of the dependent origination of the Dharma-realm is fully contained within it, it is not what is emphasized; for the urgent task of saving the age, there was no leisure for such discussion.
It is like the agada medicine, which, though possessing the power to dissolve bone, has no leisure for that purpose when the treatment of disease is urgent.

Therefore, one must not conclude that such a capacity does not exist. Furthermore, since the root of this school is said to be the "separate transmission outside the teachings," it cannot be subsumed by any vehicle—whether Hinayana, Mahayana, or any other.
It cannot be encompassed by any teaching—whether the four teachings, the five teachings, or any other.
Not only does it transcend the gradual stages, but it likewise does not abide within the sudden framework; it not only surpasses the level of the sudden, but...
Furthermore, it does not even receive the name "Perfect" (Yuan). When Xianshou categorized it as "Sudden," he did so out of necessity, merely establishing a provisional station;
how could one truly be constrained by such a classification of stages?

(18) Question: Since the arrival of Bodhidharma from the West was designated as the "Orthodox Lineage of Transmitting the Dharma," why is the Tiantai school not included among those listed in the *Chuan deng lu* (Record of the Transmission of the Lamp)?
Is this because it surpasses the Chan school, or because it has not yet lived up to the principle of "Direct Pointing"?
Answer: There are two points to this. First, because the teachings and contemplations of the Tiantai school originated earlier;
the single verse of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* is the fundamental tenet of both teaching and contemplation. Huiwen transmitted it to Huisi (Nanyue), and Nanyue transmitted it to Zhiyi (Zhizhe).

Although people were already practicing it before Bodhidharma arrived, it was specifically through Zhiyi that it was extensively propagated. Second, the teachings and contemplations of Tiantai still belong to the category of "teaching" (*jiao*).
Therefore, the single school of Bodhidharma points directly outside the teachings; as soon as one speaks of doctrinal study or contemplation, one has already deviated from the truth.

Thus, although the Tiantai teachings are most profound and subtle, they do not transcend the matters within the vehicle of the teachings. This is why the Tiantai teachings are not identical to the Chan school;
it is not because the Tiantai establishment of the Dharma is imperfect.

(19) Question: Internal precepts and external punishments differ between the monastic and the secular; internal scriptures and external classics are vastly distinct in their provisional and ultimate meanings.
How can you so extensively cite the Nine Classics and skillfully align them with the Five Punishments? Furthermore, if one does not reform despite being taught, what fault lies with the teacher?

This is the talk of village schoolmasters—like those who played the zither for their own amusement by the banks of the Chi River during the spring breeze. This is the behavior of a madman and is not appropriate.
[The opponent] introduces [the objection]: "This confuses the sacred scriptures.
[The respondent] answers: The *Lotus Sūtra* states that mundane speech, livelihoods, and so forth are all not in contradiction with the true nature (*dharmatā*).
One should know that there is no scripture that cannot be cited as proof. Furthermore, although Śākyamuni was the personal Teacher, the Six Groups and Devadatta ultimately could not be transformed;
could this not be considered the fault of the teacher? Moreover, it is merely said that playing the lute does not obstruct the worthy man.
When have I ever said that a bodhisattva must play the lute? I hope you will simply consider my underlying intent rather than merely clinging to the literal words.
(20) Question: The sutras state that Śākyamuni passed away from the Avataṃsaka world and appeared in Jambudvīpa, whereupon he preached the Dharma in ten locations.
According to one account, he was first born into the human realm and later ascended to the celestial palace to preach the Dharma.

Another states that after entering the celestial palace and preaching the *Māra-parivarta-sūtra* (or *Māra-vaśīkaraṇa-sūtra*), he descended to be born in Jambudvīpa; this implies he preached the Dharma in the celestial palace first and was subsequently born into the human world.
How are these two accounts to be reconciled?
Answer: According to the "Double Descent" (shuangchui liangxiang) chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, one knows that the essence of the Buddha is fundamentally non-dual.

While sentient beings perceive it differently, since the Buddha is able to manifest both forms simultaneously, how could he not be able to manifest both times simultaneously? This refers to his preaching the Dharma in the celestial palace.

It is also permissible for one to descend to the human realm later; this refers to attaining Buddhahood in the human realm. It is also permissible for one to ascend to the celestial palace later; this refers to having preached the Dharma in the celestial palace.
It is also permissible for one to be born in the human realm after [the celestial period] and then ascend again to the celestial palace to preach the Dharma;

this refers to attaining Buddhahood and preaching the Dharma simultaneously in both the human realm and the heavens. In such a teaching of perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*), what hindrance is there in blending the sequence of before and after? There is none.
This discourse unifies the ancient and the modern in a single breath; one need not cling to the literal text and thereby lose the underlying principle.
(21) Question: In the verse, it says "all come together to my abode. The Commentary states that this expresses that the essence all returns to the One Mind.
Now, since the mind is itself the essence, there is no principle of subsuming the essence back into the mind.

Answer: When "mind" and "activity" are discussed in opposition, the mind is the essence (*tǐ*) and activity is the function (*yòng*). When the single mind is raised alone, it is both eternally quiescent and eternally illuminating;
eternal quiescence is the essence, and eternal illumination is the function. Essence and function return to the one mind—this is like saying that the essence is here and the function is there.
One must not become mired in the word "return" and thereby doubt that the essence is subsumed within the mind. Furthermore, the Great Ultimate (*Tàijí*) is quiescent...

The Yin gives rise to life; movement gives rise to Yang. The doctrine of the Great Ultimate (*taiji*) does not yet exhaust the ultimate principle, for it still maintains that both movement and stillness are co-present.
How could the *śamatha* (calm abiding) ground of the mind fail to encompass both essence and function? If the mind were restricted solely to essence, it would stand in opposition to function.
What is meant by "one mind and three contemplations" being the Middle Way, the Supreme Truth?

(22) Question: From filial piety toward one's parents up to the ultimate Way, these should be categorized according to their respective four realms; they should not be classified as superior causes and superior fruits.
Answer: There is also this teaching regarding the division into four objects of veneration. Now, we shall take the Master’s own classification as authoritative.
If one were to divide them into four objects, why not simply state "filial piety toward parents, teachers, monks, and the Triple Gem" and then proceed directly to "the Ultimate Way"?

Why, moreover, add the two characters "filial piety" (*xiao-shun*) before "the Ultimate Way"? Furthermore, since the Dharma is already included within the Triple Gem, how could there be a "Dharma" apart from the Triple Gem?
If one has not yet exhausted the Way, yet there exists a separate Dharma of the Ultimate Way that one ought to practice with filial obedience, then the preceding three belong to the cause,
while the Ultimate Way belongs to the fruit.
(23) Question: The state has clear statutes for punishing crimes. Yet, although the killing of people is recorded in the scriptures, there is no explicit evidence [of such a crime].

When the Vaiśālī king Virūḍhaka exterminated the Śākyas, why did the Buddha not execute him? When Devadatta harmed his own brother, why did the Buddha tolerate it? Now you say that one who commits a crime may be killed; if so, what offense does the executioner commit?
To falsely harm living beings violates the Buddha’s regulations and instructions. As it was said of old: "When a non-Buddhist enters into the Buddha-dharma, he must..."
Is this not the proof that [the state] destroys the Buddha-dharma? I pray you will dispel my confusion. Answer:
Killing when one perceives the [karmic] opportunity is based on the *Shu-wen* (Commentary). The *Shu-wen* is itself based on the Buddha’s own teachings; it is not a product of mere conjecture.

Indeed, while the śramaṇas are dedicated exclusively to the practice of compassion, kings and ministers hold the authority over life and death. This distinction between their respective roles is clearly elucidated in the *Fa-yin* (Exposition of the Hidden).

Now, one might ask: Is the Buddha of the class of śramaṇas, or of the class of kings and ministers? How can you cite the cases of Vimalakīrti and Devadatta to prove that killing is not [a transgression]?
Furthermore, the precept against killing for kings and ministers is not only distinct from that of śramaṇas; it is also different from that of commoners.
To kill one who is guilty constitutes a transgression; thus, such a king or minister will never have a day upon which they receive the precepts.

Therefore, when Master Guī conferred the precepts upon the mountain deity, he did not prohibit the act of killing itself; he only prohibited the inflicting of unjust punishments and the taking of innocent life.
It does not prohibit the acquisition of wealth; it only prohibits seeking power and fortune through the performance of sacrifices. It does not prohibit marriage;
it only prohibits the pursuit of desire that violates the great human relations. It does not prohibit speech; it only prohibits falsehood that contravenes the Will of Heaven.
It does not prohibit drinking and feasting; it only prohibits excessive indulgence that ruins upright affairs.

To preach the Dharma in such a manner is called following capacities and adapting to conditions without overstepping the bounds; undergoing a thousand transformations and ten thousand changes without departing from the mind.
It is appropriate both in adversity and prosperity, benefiting both monastics and laypeople alike. Above, it accords with the thousand sages; below, it delivers the myriad beings. Alas!
If every person acts as an "outsider" (tīrthika) in this way, will not the Buddha-Dharma flourish ever more?

(24) Question: "The enmity of one's lord or father must be avenged; this is a provisional teaching (*upāya*). Once the *Nanjing* (Inner Classic) is promulgated, provisional teachings shall be abolished.
How can you again cite the precedents of Chen Heng and Zhao Dun, thereby contravening the words of Śākyamuni and Zhiyi?
Regardless of whether they were kings or ministers, [such acts] should surely be entirely prohibited."

Answer: Confucian scholars do not take pleasure in the Buddha-dharma precisely because of people such as these. What is there to wonder at in the fact that, throughout past and present, they slander the monastics, saying they have "no father and no ruler"?
Furthermore, since even Confucius himself could not execute Chen Heng, what can be expected of the rebellious ministers and treacherous sons of the world?
I only fear that people will not receive the Bodhisattva precepts. Why is this? If those who receive the precepts are firm, then those who practice evil will find it difficult [to prevail].
Thus, these Bodhisattva precepts are a resource for the restoration of order. The Buddha-dharma is perfect and subtle; it integrates the mundane and the supramundane without obstruction.
Yet, when deluded people cling to it, the resulting calamity reaches such a state—how can one help but lament! This has already been addressed in my *Fayi* (Unfolding the Hidden).
This has been clarified through retrospective analysis; it need not be elaborated upon further here.

(25) Question: To bestow the precepts by reflecting the shadow of a lamp and to dismantle the altar upon seeing the light of the sun—revealing secrets in darkness and transmitting them in obscurity, gathering at night and dispersing at dawn—does this not cause people to increase their confusion?
Answer: The Son of Heaven is attended at dawn with the five drums; Confucius is sacrificed to under the clear night sky. I have never heard it said that these increase one’s confusion.
Mencius spoke of the "clear and bright qi of the night," while Master Deng remarked that "the daylight is noisy and chaotic. I pray you, consider these two views together.

(26) Question: What harm does the playful pursuit of calligraphy and ink-washing do to the *vinaya*? If it can be understood as such, there ought to be a distinct transgression; yet this has nothing to do with poetry or painting.
Whether one ceases or abandons them, we have never heard of anyone falling [into hell] on that account. Why then do you hastily offer such criticism?

If you insist that every single person must be a Lu Neng, I fear that everyone will instead become a Xi Zhai. To judge by the eyes is called "pure eyes," but to delude the mind is merely called "purity."
[The interlocutor says: "How tragic! The Empty King (the Buddha) has no more days to appear in the provisional realm. [The Master] replies:

"This does not mean that poetry must necessarily be written by one with white leprosy, nor that painting must necessarily be done by one with *nirbali* [a skin disease]. Poetry and painting do not provide salvation for the two individuals in their distress.
What I am saying is simply this: those who have become monks should study the Way; they should not engage in miscellaneous studies. Alas! If this is indeed the case, then the situation is clarified.
The mind. When one pushes beyond oneself to save others, it is like performing on whatever stage presents itself; there is nothing that cannot be done.

If this were not so, I fear you would fail to let go of the mind and close your eyes. If you are willing to open your eyes and resolve the matter for everyone, and to awaken the deluded mind in each person, I can guarantee that the five eyes will be perfectly clear and the thousand spirits will be thoroughly penetrating.
Furthermore, when a Bodhisattva emerges from the provisional state, they extensively practice the six perfections and ten thousand virtues.

To practice [the Way] and universally deliver the four modes of birth within the nine realms is merely to chant verses about the moon and compose rhapsodies on flowers, or to depict mountains and paint waters;

the merit of clarifying the Way is not immediate, and how can the transformation that benefits all be accomplished? How sublime is the Teacher of Gods and Humans, who does not emerge from such mere conventions!
(27) Question: The sutras state that one’s body shall be crushed by iron hammers; one must never accept the prostrations of others with a body that has violated the precepts.
Now, if one feels ashamed because the virtue of one's precepts cannot be fully maintained, yet still expects disciples to perform prostrations before them, this is already the lowest of strategies.
Who is called a superior person (*uttamapuruṣa*)? Answer:

One who possesses no virtue yet considers themselves humble; one who strictly follows the Buddha’s regulations. Conversely, one who deceives the world and deludes their superiors with self-importance is a rebel against the sagely teachings.
Such a person is neither a superior person nor even a person who avoids transgression. Although emerging with an inferior strategy is still better than having no strategy at all, even so—

Indeed, there are those whose station is ever higher yet whose minds are ever more humble; they do not slight those who have attained the rank of Bodhisattva, but instead pay universal homage to the fourfold assembly.
It cannot be that their precepts and virtue are incomplete, for even Yu of Xia, while personally serving as King, would promptly bow before a single word of righteous counsel.

One should feel ashamed of these many faults. This is truly because there is originally no fixed dharma between the provisional and the ultimate; each degree of elevation or depression has its own appropriate place.
When the time comes to occupy the position of rectitude to serve as a "southern guide" for later students, then it is fitting that Ciming sits calmly while accepting his prostrations.
When the time comes to exalt the profound Way to awaken the arrogance of the madman, then it is fitting that Master Zang bows low.
It may also be permissible to avoid bowing. The wondrous application is not constant; indeed, it cannot be lightly discussed. (28) Question:
When the Thousand-Petal Buddha personally preached the sutra, all people were able to receive the precepts, with the sole exception of those who have committed the seven heinous offenses.
Who established the three tiers? Do not cite provisional texts to obstruct those who possess the capacity for the perfect [teaching]. Furthermore, it is said that even laypeople...
One must first receive the five precepts. Yet, in the sūtras, the sequence of ranks is listed with kings and ministers at the head.
This suggests that kings and ministers may perhaps receive them directly. Answer:

The parable of the multi-storied pavilion was spoken from the Golden Mouth; these wholesome precepts and rules are not of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna). Even for those of perfect capacity, they must abide by the established order.
The regulation states: If one must receive [the precepts] directly, there is also a skillful means by which one may receive them directly without violating the sequential order.

This is as follows: within a single day, first receive the five precepts, and then subsequently receive the bodhisattva precepts. For those who have left the household life, it is likewise within a single day.
First one receives the ten precepts, followed by the full ordination and the bodhisattva precepts; although these are said to be received directly, they do not bypass the proper sequence.
How could this apply only to kings and ministers? It may be practiced by all—monastics and laypeople alike.
(29) Question: The precepts of the Buddha are words of absolute necessity. Yet you reveal hidden flaws by proposing claims that are not necessarily so.

If you say there is no attachment, why then do you insist on such rigorous adherence? As for serving the assembly like a slave, or cutting one’s own flesh to feed a hawk—these are all actual occurrences.
Why then do you say they are not necessarily so?

Answer: It is not necessarily so. To say "not necessarily" does not mean it is absolutely impossible. Why? If one must become a slave for the sake of serving the Buddha, then the common people would have no sovereign.
If one must cut off one's own flesh for the sake of saving sentient beings, then beginners would have no intact skin.

If one who is a Dharma Master must preach the sutras, then the fivefold practice of the *Lotus Sutra* is abandoned; if one who eats daily must consume two or three catties, then they are comparable to He Zeng’s ten thousand coins.
If, among people today, one must have no prophetic revelation as their teacher, then the worthy person will ultimately have no teacher at all.
If, in the present time, one must necessarily offer sacrifices in order to attain deliverance, then the poor would never attain it. Such cases are those where the necessity is not absolute.
Where there is this lack of necessity, that which is necessary can remain constant. Without this lack of necessity, that which is necessary would be exhausted.
When exhausted, there is change; through change, there is penetration; through penetration, there is permanence—both in the mundane world and the world-transcending realm.
The interval is one and the same. (30) Question: Lay practitioners also lecture on the sutras at times; may they still transmit the precepts and act as masters?
Answer: This depends on their own realization. If a Confucian attains enlightenment in the Buddha-way, it does not hinder them from being a master for the monastics of the world. But if a monastic...

One who clarifies the sagely learning may serve as a teacher for the Confucian scholars of the world. Were it otherwise, their respective fields of study would be specialized and their academic lineages distinct:

the arts of self-cultivation, family regulation, state governance, and bringing peace to the world should belong to the "Sovereign King" (Confucius), while the rituals of *karmavācanā* and *poṣadha* revert to the monastic community alone.
(31) Question: If all those who have not received the precepts are termed "evil persons," then those close at hand—śrāmaṇeras and bhikṣus—are startled to be so designated.
Those far removed—Yao, Shun, the Duke of Zhou, and Confucius—are indiscriminately subjected to this name.
Furthermore, Emperor Yang of Sui surpassed Wen and Jing, and Fang Rong excelled Yao and Song; these are truly points I cannot comprehend.

Answer: There are two meanings to this. First is the meaning of relative opposition. Those who have not yet received the precepts are all termed "evil," just as those who have not yet ascended to the stage of the noble ones (ārya) are all termed "ordinary" (pṛthagjana);
this is not the evil of being cruel or wicked. Furthermore, the Dharma of the Buddha always surpasses worldly dharmas;
thus, even those who are virtuous people in the world are still termed "evil" within the Buddha-dharma, and those who are sages in the world—[are likewise so termed].
Within the Buddha-dharma, such a person is still termed an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). Second is the sense of exhortation: not receiving the precepts is itself an evil;

this clarifies that the precepts must absolutely be received. Based on these two meanings, although Yao, Shun, the Duke of Zhou, and Confucius did not receive the precepts, they did not fail to be sages of the world.
If the rulers of the Sui dynasty had been made to maintain the precepts until the end of their lives, how could they have merely surpassed Emperors Wen and Jing?
He surpasses Yao and Song alone! (32) Question:
Yuanwu and Gao’an formed separate factions and established their own parties; each of the two houses led their own disciples. How could these two elders have been without their partisans?
That the struggle remains so firm even now is truly because the Elder [Zhaozhou] was so inclusive and tolerant that Maitreya has long remained delayed.
Seeking fame, you, Master, have not yet transcended the desire for victory; do not shield the shortcomings of former sages, but rather open the delusions of later students.
Answer: Even Lin Xiangru endured private enmity, and Liu Yuancheng did not lose his harmonious spirit. As for Yuanwu and Gaoyuan—

"Successing the patriarchs and transmitting the lamp, propagating the transformation of the Buddha in his stead—yet there still remains this very thing. How can one be called a person of 'the other shore'?

Is it not as if Danzhu’s idle wandering were used to blame Emperor Yao for lacking righteous instruction, or Ran Qiu’s amassing of wealth were used to criticize Confucius for failing in his good teaching?
Is it not as if the Six Groups’ disordering of virtue and the Two Assemblies’ dividing of the river were used to [accuse] Śākyamuni?"
Is it not that you cannot help but desire to prevail? Nevertheless, there may be those who uphold the correct doctrine and support the Buddha’s grace during the Dharma-ending age;
such persons must not avoid minor slights at the expense of losing sight of the greater purpose. A Bodhisattva has no fear of ill repute—let the heroic-minded consider this.
(33) Question: The teachings and contemplations of a single school have explained the Three Truths through the scriptures, following one another down to the present day without any divergent views.
Yet it is said that the Master of the Commentary himself did not adhere to a fixed doctrine; how could his disciples have falsely opened up alternative paths?
Now, as for the supreme Dharma of the Middle Way, how far apart could they possibly be? Why then do you use this to criticize Zhangan and Jingxi? What else can one expect from such a person?
[Question: Is this the Longshui [commentary] on the Wēnlíng [edition]? [Answer:
"Not adhering to dharmas" means to penetrate dharmas without being obstructed; it does not mean to discard dharmas and fail to employ them. The commentary states:
"All the supreme dharmas of bodhisattvas are termed 'the primary meaning' (paramārtha). The meaning of the word "all" (*fan*) is self-evident. There is none...
As for what is questionable: furthermore, the three truths (trīṇi satyāni) originally arose from the Buddha’s teachings; how could they truly have been propounded by Tiantai alone?
These teachings are common to all schools; how could they belong exclusively to the Tiantai school? Therefore, every dharma is a truth, and every truth comprises the three.

Even when one does not explicitly speak of the "three truths," the three truths are nonetheless fully present. Thus, it is certainly not necessary to exhaustively cite every single word or phrase from the sūtras and śāstras.

To definitively adjudicate the three truths as if they were fixed assignments is like arranging them in a rigid order; it is not the discourse of a person of comprehensive understanding, but is called "clinging to dharmas.
This has already been repeatedly investigated and clarified in the forty-first section on minor defilements of the *Fayi* (Unfolding the Hidden); I request that you examine this further in detail.

Furthermore, both Zhanran (Zhang’an) and Jingxi did not cling to dharmas, nor is there anything to be criticized in them. As time passed, successive generations established their own distinct schools and lineages.
To engage in excessive discrimination leads only to entanglement and obstruction. Let us set aside the two masters, Wēnlíng and Chángshuǐ; how could they possibly be faulted?
Indeed, it is certainly not the case that the ancients were invariably superior to those of today, nor is it the case that those of today are invariably inferior to the ancients.
Even if there be slight flaws, what is wrong with examining them with an impartial mind and discussing them together? It is simply that one should not seek out hidden defects.

They seek out faults, fearing only that they are not deep enough; they are like vengeful families instigating lawsuits, exhaustively reviling and utterly denigrating, fearing only that they are not sufficiently satisfying—like drunkards cursing in the streets.
This is a sign of the decay of the age and a portent of the extinction of the Dharma. Should one not be on guard against it?

A golden ring was fastened around the pig's neck, and it lay beneath a wall to the west of the street. Sengcong knocked on the wall and asked whose butcher shop it was. The man replied, "It belongs to Master Zhao.
He asked what the name of this [pig] was, and the man said, "Bohe. "Because he eats only bohe," [the man continued], "I slaughter a thousand or ten thousand pigs every day."
The boar was wild and difficult to restrain; by using this pig as a guide, the others followed one after another to their deaths.

The *Tulāyūji jibao en jing* (Sutra on Tulāyūji Repaying Kindness by Healing Illness) states: When the Buddha was at the Bamboo Grove Monastery, there was a bhikṣu suffering from a malignant ulcer for which he was loathed and despised by the community.
The Tathāgata went to his room and, extending his hand of *tūla-cotton*, massaged and washed him; the sores on his body were all [healed].
He recovered.

Yu Xiang of Jin was in a precarious situation with his life at stake during a great epidemic in the Xianning era of Emperor Wu of Jin; two of his elder brothers had both died, and his younger brother Bian was again in danger.
It was perilous; the miasma of the pestilence was raging fiercely. His parents and brothers all went out to stay in the outer quarters, but Xiang alone remained and would not leave.
Although his paternal uncles and elder brothers urged him to go, he said, "By nature I do not fear illness," and so he personally attended to him, never sleeping day or night.
After more than ten days, the epidemic subsided; the family members then returned home. Zhenbian’s illness was cured, and Xiang was likewise free from ailment.
The elders all said, "How extraordinary this son is! He maintains what others cannot maintain and practices what others cannot practice."
Only after the cold of winter does one know that the pine and cypress are the last to wither. Thus it was first known that pestilence could not infect him.
